blocks.text: First Corinthians 14 addresses the exercise of spiritual gifts in assembly, particularly the contrast between tongues and prophecy. Paul argues for intelligible communication and edification of the gathered church. The chapter assumes women participate in prayer and prophecy while establishing regulations for intelligibility, turn-taking, and evaluation of what is spoken. Throughout, the concern centers on building up the assembly, enabling learning and encouragement, and maintaining peace and order conducive to these ends.

Since the Corinthians are zealous for spiritual gifts, Paul directs their zeal toward building up the church. A tongue speaker should pray for the ability to interpret, because praying in a tongue—though the spirit prays—leaves understanding unfruitful. Paul resolves this tension through a personal commitment: he will pray with both spirit and mind, sing with both spirit and understanding. This is not a rejection of spiritual experience but an insistence that Spirit and intellect work together in assembly contexts. Intelligible instruction, translation, and informed participation do not quench the Spirit but complete it.

Paul introduces the scenario of an uninitiated person or unbeliever entering the assembly. If everyone is speaking in tongues, the visitor hears undifferentiated sounds and judges the assembly mad. By contrast, if prophecy is spoken, even an outsider hears intelligible words that may disclose the secrets of their heart and lead them to acknowledge God's presence. This is not a mandate for spectacular display or invasive disclosure but a recognition that intelligible, truthful speech can have genuine spiritual impact while unintelligible noise alienates and confuses.

Paul affirms plural participation: the gathered assembly may have contributions of psalms, teachings, revelations, and tongues, all aimed at building up. He then sets limits on prophetic speech: two or three may speak in sequence while others evaluate what is said. If someone else receives a revelation, the first speaker must yield, keeping silent. Prophetic spirits remain subject to prophets—the gift does not override the speaker's agency or the assembly's need to discern. This structure prevents both chaos and monopoly, enabling multiple voices while maintaining accountability and intelligibility.

Verses 34-35 direct women to remain silent in churches and ask questions at home. Textually, all Greek manuscripts include these verses, though some Western witnesses place them after verse 40. Within the chapter's ordering sequence, the verb 'silence' is applied to three distinct scenarios: when a tongue speaker lacks an interpreter, when a prophet is displaced by another's revelation, and in the disputed verses regarding women. This parallel structure suggests contextual regulation rather than an absolute gender ban. The same letter assumes women pray and prophesy in assembly. Interpreting these verses requires textual transparency and acknowledgment that their precise scope and application remain disputed.

sections.title: The Nature of Tongues and Interpretation

blocks.text: Tongues in the Corinthian assembly are described through prayer, praise, mystery, sounds with meaning, possible interpretation, self-edification, and outsider incomprehension. No surviving audio sample exists, nor does the text offer a single exclusive classification. Acts 2 narrates intelligible multilingual speech where hearers recognize native languages, a description distinct from the Corinthian situation. The diversity of descriptions prevents any single modern practice or ancient parallel from predetermining what occurred in Corinth. The chapter's focus remains not on phonetic analysis but on whether assembly speech serves mutual edification and intelligible building up.
